# Household Budget Midyear Review

## Summary
The two of us sat down in the first week of July to check where the household money had actually gone across the first six months of the year. We picked July because the summer is expensive and we wanted the numbers in front of us before the holiday spending started rather than after. The picture was broadly healthy, with the surplus landing roughly where we had hoped and no nasty surprises hidden in the small print. We keep our accounts separate and pay into a joint pot for the shared costs, which works well enough as long as we sit down like this twice a year. What stood out was how many fixed things had quietly crept up since January without either of us really noticing. Subscriptions were the clearest example, and they were the first thing we changed once the totals were in front of us. The rest of the review confirmed that the boring parts of the plan were holding, which is exactly what we wanted to see at the halfway mark. Nothing here is dramatic, and that is the point of a halfway check like this one.

## Spending
Groceries were the biggest single line on the joint account, tracking 445 EUR a month across the six months, a little above the four hundred we had pencilled in during January. We put the gap down to two things: prices at the till and one too many mid-week top-up trips that always cost more than the weekly shop. Transport came to 120 EUR a month, mostly the train for the commute and the odd taxi when the weather was foul, and that felt fair for the distance involved. Housing costs held steady and we had no repairs to speak of, which is always a relief in a flat of this age. Utilities were seasonal but averaged out close to plan. The subscriptions line was the one that made us wince: nine separate services, several of which one of us had signed up for and the other had forgotten about entirely. Dining out ran a shade high in the spring, when there seemed to be a birthday every other weekend. The household repairs fund went untouched for the whole stretch, which we took as a good sign. Everything else sat within a few euros of the plan. The garden spend was a small line, a few trays of seedlings and a bag of compost, and it saved more than it cost given how much we ate from the beds over the summer. Books and hobbies sat within the envelope we had agreed. We noticed that food waste was creeping up in the early weeks, so we started planning the meals for the week on Sunday evening before the shopping, which cut both the waste and the bill. That alone accounts for a fair slice of why the grocery overspend was less bad than it first looked.

## Adjustments
Subscriptions were the first fix, and we cut from nine down to six by cancelling the three neither of us had opened in months. That brought the line to 42 EUR a month, a saving we felt immediately because it was pure waste rather than anything we enjoyed. We moved the monthly surplus out of the current account and into the savings account the day after payday, so it stops being available for casual spending before we have thought about it. We also redid the standing orders from scratch, because over a couple of years of small edits they had drifted into a shape neither of us could explain. The groceries spend gets a proper weekly shop rather than the top-up trips that always cost more. We agreed to look at the dining out line again after the summer, since we both enjoy it and neither of us wants to cut it to nothing. Transport we left alone. The point of the exercise was to trim the waste without touching the things that make the month pleasant. We also set a rule that any subscription over a certain size gets a question before renewal, rather than rolling over quietly the way they had until now. The cuts are small in cash but large in tidiness, which matters more than the money on a line like this one.

## Notes
We will do the next one of these in January rather than waiting the full year, since the midyear catch-up caught more than we expected. The joint pot needs a slightly larger monthly contribution from both of us to cover the higher grocery prices, and we agreed on that without much argument. I keep the running totals in a shared sheet, and for once the other half actually opens it, which helps. The one thing we did not resolve is whether the holiday should come out of the joint pot or our own money, so we are leaving that until the summer trip is over and the actual figure is known. Otherwise, calm halfway point. The shared sheet has been the single best change of the year, because seeing the same numbers keeps us from arguing about a feeling rather than a fact. We have both agreed to log spending the same day rather than at the end of the month, when the receipts have gone missing. If the second half holds to the first, we will be in good shape for the winter.
